How can researchers work effectively with an AI coding agent—and
critically evaluate its results? This interactive Hackathon uses epidemic
forecasting to explore the research workflow: framing questions, giving
instructions, reviewing code, challenging assumptions, and evaluating
results.

Starting with eight observations recorded at two-week intervals from a
real measles outbreak, participants will work with Nguyen Tran using
OpenAI Codex to explore the data, identify missing information, consider
up to three candidate models, and forecast the remaining eight
observations. Human scientific judgment will guide each stage.

## Who this is for

All experience levels are welcome. No advanced programming skills or
individual Codex access are required. The main workflow will be
facilitator-led, so everyone can join the discussion and scientific
review. Participants who wish to run the Codex workflow on their own
computers will need their own Codex access and the setup described below.

## What you will learn

By the end of the session, you will be able to:

1. Describe a practical workflow for collaborating with an AI coding
   agent in scientific research.
2. Understand how a coding-agent workflow differs from a conventional
   chatbot conversation.
3. Identify where human guidance, code review, and scientific judgment
   are essential.
4. Explain the difference between fitting observed data and forecasting
   unseen observations.
5. Recognise how limited data and analytical assumptions affect
   predictions and uncertainty.
6. Explain why evaluation criteria should be agreed before withheld
   observations are revealed.
7. Recognise the importance of reproducibility, held-out validation,
   and preventing data leakage.
8. Critically assess AI-generated results, distinguishing evidence
   from assumptions and hindsight.

## Before the session

Bring a computer with a reliable internet connection and access to the
free version of ChatGPT for accompanying activities. The opening exercise
uses CSV upload and data analysis; if those capabilities are unavailable
in your account, follow the demonstration.

To run the full workflow yourself, also prepare:

- Codex access, signed in and able to open a local project folder;
- a working Python environment with NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and Matplotlib
  available to Codex; and
- Git, optionally, to record your own forecast checkpoint.

Download and extract the starter ZIP into a new folder. It contains only
`WORKSHOP_BRIEF.md` and `data/observed.csv`. Keep a separate copy for the
opening plotting demonstration, then use a fresh starter copy for the
formal challenge. Open that extracted folder in Codex rather than the
whole Hackathon repository, which contains materials from other sessions.
You do not need to install Quarto to follow the lab.

## Session outline

The two-hour session moves through six stages:

1. **Compare workflows:** use ChatGPT and Codex to explore the same data,
   examining context, tools, and saved project files.
2. **Establish project rules:** document known evidence, missing
   information, and the boundary around withheld observations; check
   that a fresh session can recover the saved context.
3. **Review a scientific plan:** select at most three candidate models
   with explicit assumptions, uncertainty, and diagnostic checks.
4. **Implement and inspect:** watch the agent write and run code,
   resolve errors, produce figures, and examine sensitivity to an
   important assumption.
5. **Freeze and evaluate:** agree on evaluation criteria and save the
   forecasts and uncertainty estimates before the facilitator releases
   biweeks 9–16. Compare the frozen predictions with those observations.
6. **Conduct a scientific postmortem:** discuss what worked, what
   failed, and how assumptions shaped the results, preserving the
   distinction between prior reasoning and hindsight.

The target is reported cases, not all infections. Population size,
vaccination coverage, reporting completeness, and other community
metadata are not supplied. Model choice remains open; participants are
not required to use an SIR model. A convincing fit to the rising segment
does not establish that a model will forecast the future well.

::: {.callout-important title="Preserve the forecasting challenge"}
Use only the supplied observations before the reveal. Do not search for
the original outbreak or unreleased outcomes. The facilitator will
supply the withheld observations after forecasts have been frozen.
:::

## About the instructor

Dr. Tran Dang Nguyen is the founder of the Center for Computational
Epidemiology and Infectious Diseases (CEID) in Vietnam, established
following his tenure as a Research Assistant Professor at Temple
University and Penn State University. He earned his PhD from The Open
University, UK, in 2016, focusing on individual-based simulations to
combat the spread of antimalarial drug resistance.

During his doctoral and postdoctoral work, Dr. Nguyen developed and
validated a microsimulation model for malaria, used to evaluate
strategies including multiple first-line therapies, triple
artemisinin-based combination therapies (TACTs), and mass drug
administration (MDA). His research has informed policy decisions in
Uganda, Rwanda, and Tanzania.

The participant guide and starter materials were supplied by Nguyen Tran
for this session.
